question: In the lecture, the norm of a partition is defined as the length of the longest subinterval. Explain why this definition is used and how it affects the construction of the Riemann sum for a continuous function \(f\) on \([A,B]\) when the tags are chosen to be the right endpoints of the subintervals.
answer: The norm, \(\|P\| = \max_i (x_i - x_{i-1})\), measures the mesh size of the partition. By requiring \(\|P\|\) to become arbitrarily small, we ensure that each subinterval is small enough that the value of a continuous function \(f\) does not vary much within it. When the tags are taken as the right endpoints, the Riemann sum is \(\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})\). As \(\|P\| \to 0\), the difference between \(f\) evaluated at any point in \([x_{i-1},x_i]\) and at the right endpoint \(x_i\) tends to zero by continuity, so the Riemann sums converge to the integral \(\int_A^B f(x)\,dx\). Thus, the norm controls the refinement of the partition, and the choice of right‑endpoint tags provides a concrete, consistent way to sample \(f\) on each subinterval.

question: In the lecture, explain why making the norm of a partition arbitrarily small ensures that the corresponding Riemann sums approximate the area under the curve of a continuous function \(f\) on \([A,B]\). Discuss how the choice of tags (for example, taking all tags to be right endpoints) affects the Riemann sum, and state the precise condition that guarantees the convergence of these sums to the Riemann integral of \(f\).
answer: Because \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([A,B]\), it is uniformly continuous. Hence for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that whenever \(|x-y|<\delta\) we have \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\). If the norm of a partition \(P\) is less than \(\delta\), then every subinterval has length \(<\delta\), so the value of \(f\) at any point in the subinterval differs from the value at the chosen tag by less than \(\varepsilon\). Consequently the Riemann sum \(S(f,P,\tau)=\sum f(\tau_i)\Delta x_i\) differs from the integral \(\int_A^B f(x)\,dx\) by at most \(\varepsilon\) times the total length \(B-A\). Thus, as the norm tends to zero, the sums converge to the integral. The specific choice of tags (right endpoints, left endpoints, midpoints, or any point in each subinterval) does not affect the limit for a continuous function; all such Riemann sums converge to the same value. The precise convergence condition is: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that if \(\|P\|<\delta\) then \(|S(f,P,\tau)-\int_A^B f(x)\,dx|<\varepsilon\).

question: In the lecture, the modulus of continuity \(\omega(\eta)\) of a continuous function \(f\) on \([a,b]\) is defined as the supremum of \(|f(x)-f(y)|\) for \(|x-y|<\eta\). Suppose \(P\) and \(P'\) are tagged partitions of \([a,b]\) with \(P'\) finer than \(P\). Explain how \(\omega(\eta)\) can be used to bound the difference between the Riemann sums \(S(f,P')\) and \(S(f,P)\), and why this bound tends to zero as the mesh of \(P'\) tends to zero.
answer:
For each subinterval \([x_{i-1},x_i]\) of the coarser partition \(P\), the finer partition \(P'\) subdivides it into smaller subintervals \([x_{i-1},x_{i-1}^1], [x_{i-1}^1,x_{i-1}^2],\dots,[x_{i-1}^{k-1},x_i]\). Let \(\eta\) be the mesh of \(P'\), i.e. the maximum length of these subintervals. For any tag \(t_i\) of \(P\) and any tag \(t_j'\) of a subinterval of \(P'\) lying inside \([x_{i-1},x_i]\), we have \(|t_i-t_j'|<\eta\). Hence \(|f(t_i)-f(t_j')|\le \omega(\eta)\). The contribution of the subinterval \([x_{i-1},x_i]\) to the difference \(S(f,P')-S(f,P)\) is therefore bounded in absolute value by \(\omega(\eta)\,(x_i-x_{i-1})\). Summing over all subintervals of \(P\) gives
    \[
      |S(f,P')-S(f,P)| \;\le\; \omega(\eta)\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-x_{i-1}) \;=\; \omega(\eta)\,(b-a).
    \]
    Since \(f\) is continuous, \(\omega(\eta)\to 0\) as \(\eta\to 0\). Thus, as the mesh of the finer partition \(P'\) tends to zero, the bound \(\omega(\eta)(b-a)\) tends to zero, forcing the Riemann sums \(S(f,P')\) and \(S(f,P)\) to become arbitrarily close. This demonstrates how the modulus of continuity controls the convergence of Riemann sums when one partition is refined.

Thus the absolute value of the telescoping sum is bounded by the sum of the absolute values of its terms.
